The SHM1 airfoil was designed to meet the requirements of the small-business Honda Jet.
The SHM1 airfoil has undergone extensive testing across various operational conditions, including low-speed wind tunnel tests and flight tests.
The study simulated a range of free-stream Mach numbers (0.134, 0.31, 0.62, 0.72, 0.73, 0.78) and Reynolds numbers (4.8 × 10^6 to 16.2 × 10^6).
The numerical simulations employed a shock-free mesh to accurately capture the dynamics of traveling waves in compressible flow around airfoils.
For the low speed condition (M_s = 0.134), the time-series of vorticity revealed a singular time period associated with Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex shedding.
At the climb condition (M_s = 0.31), the time-series of vorticity showed the presence of multiple time periods due to interactions between Kutta waves and trailing edge vortices.
At the cruise condition (M_s = 0.62), the time-series and associated spectrum demonstrated a chaotic, multi-periodic nature of the flow, with no discernible peaks in the frequency plane.

For the off-design transonic conditions, the emergence of shocks led to complex shock-boundary layer interactions, exhibiting large-amplitude, low-frequency pressure fluctuations on the airfoil surface.
The study found that as the free-stream Mach number increased, the magnitude of vorticity generation increased, and the Fourier amplitude was redistributed across a wider range of frequencies.
The steepest pressure spike was observed for the M_s = 0.78 case, which demonstrated the largest separated region and shock extent.

The skin friction coefficient analysis showed that for the low speed and climb conditions, there was either no separation or a very short separation bubble, while the off-design transonic conditions exhibited more significant separation.
The study provided benchmark results for optimization of various flow separation and shock control techniques for natural laminar airfoils like the SHM1.
The numerical methods used in this study have been previously validated against experimental data from flight tests and wind tunnel results.
The study highlights the necessity for a comprehensive assessment of the aerodynamic performance of natural laminar flow airfoils under both design and off-design conditions.
The findings contribute to the design of optimized natural laminar flow airfoils by providing insights into boundary layer characteristics and unsteady separation.
